content: 1. Reports on product stewardship activities related to compliance with the International Code of Conduct on Pesticide Management should be submitted by the pesticide industry to the Directors-General of the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) and the World Health Organization (WHO), as well as to the Executive Director of the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP). 2. Non-governmental organizations (NGOs) and other interested entities are encouraged to monitor activities associated with the implementation of the Code and report their findings to the Directors-General of FAO and WHO, and the Executive Director of UNEP. 3. The governing bodies of FAO, WHO, and UNEP are advised to periodically review the relevance and effectiveness of the Code. The Code should be treated as a dynamic document, updated as necessary to reflect advancements in technical, economic, and social domains. 4. International policy instruments addressing various aspects of the pesticide life cycle include operational frameworks such as the Codex Alimentarius (specifically the Codex Committee on Pesticide Residues, active since 1966), the Montreal Protocol on Substances that Deplete the Ozone Layer (adopted in 1987 and effective from 1989), the Basel Convention on the Control of Transboundary Movements of Hazardous Wastes and Their Disposal (adopted in 1989 and effective from 1992), the Rotterdam Convention on the Prior Informed Consent Procedure for Certain Hazardous Chemicals and Pesticides in International Trade (adopted in 1998 and effective from 2004), and the Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants (adopted in 2001 and effective from 2004). 5. Broader policy instruments providing a general context for pesticide management include the ILO Convention on Safety and Health in Agriculture (adopted in 2001 and effective from 2003), the ILO Convention on Safety in the Use of Chemicals at Work (adopted in 1990 and effective from 1993), the Convention on the Prohibition and Immediate Action for the Elimination of the Worst Forms of Child Labour (adopted in 1999), the Rio Declaration on Environment and Development (1992), Agenda 21 (1992), the Convention on Biological Diversity (adopted in 1992 and effective from 1993), the ILO Convention on the Prevention of Major Industrial Accidents (adopted in 1993 and effective from 1997), the Rome Declaration on World Food Security and the World Food Summit Plan of Action (1996), the WHO World Health Declaration (1998), the Strategic Approach to International Chemicals Management (adopted in 2006), and the Globally Harmonized System for the Classification and Labelling of Chemicals. 6. Guidelines and technical resources for pesticide management include FAO and WHO documents on pesticide labeling, application practices, personal protection, resistance management, efficacy evaluation, and environmental criteria. These also include manuals for inventory-taking, storage, disposal, and the prevention of obsolete pesticide stock accumulation. 7. Specific international guidelines address the registration, certification, and testing of pesticides and their application equipment, as well as the organization of training schemes for pesticide operators. These guidelines are designed to ensure compliance with safety, environmental, and public health standards. 8. The FAO and WHO have developed resources for monitoring pesticide-related health and environmental incidents, as well as for diagnosing and treating pesticide poisoning. These tools aim to enhance the sound management of pesticides and mitigate associated risks. 9. The OECD has established principles for good laboratory practices and guidelines for the submission and evaluation of data on plant protection products and their active substances. These frameworks support regulatory compliance and the harmonization of international standards. 10. The WHO has issued recommendations for the classification of pesticides by hazard, along with guidelines for their safe use. These recommendations are complemented by the United Nations' model regulations for the transport of dangerous goods.
